strengths: The paper targets a relevant problem: influence objectives may involve heterogeneous counterfactual utilities that change with network exposure. Combining causal interference modeling with hypergraph influence maximization could be valuable. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/neurips2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-tcd39lty/call-ddf626be79c64e22a5a0c67044b6ab62/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
It attempts an end-to-end treatment, including a formal objective, greedy and accelerated algorithms, theoretical bounds, and experiments on several network topologies.
A-CauIM reports substantial wall-clock reductions relative to the authors' simulation-based implementation while sometimes retaining similar reported objective values.
The work explicitly considers signed treatment effects and estimation noise. A code link is provided, and no new human-subject intervention is reported.
weaknesses: The central causal-identification claim is unsupported. Assumption 2.2 asserts independence between potential outcomes rather than treatment ignorability; positivity, overlap, and a justified exposure mapping are absent. Because surrounding treatments are generated by the seed-dependent diffusion, fitting an MLP to one factual outcome per node does not recover individual counterfactual effects. At most, much stronger assumptions could identify conditional average effects.

The objective is incoherent for environment-dependent effects. Realized utility should involve the joint expectation E[1{node i is activated} tau_i(T)], whereas the paper effectively multiplies activation probability by an effect depending on that same random activation environment. The needed factorization conflicts with the paper's motivation, and the intervention represented by seeding is not clearly connected to the treatment whose effect is estimated.

The influence algebra underlying the theory is incorrect. The identity ap(v;S)=sum_{u in S} pr(u,v), and similarly Equation 7, double-counts outcomes reachable from multiple seeds. Thus the marginal formulas in Equations 8-9 and the subsequent proof do not represent IC/SICP spread.

The claimed 1-1/e guarantee treats node effects as fixed weights, although the principal contribution assumes they change with the seed-dependent environment. Even positive set-dependent weights need not yield monotonicity or submodularity. The cited augmented-graph argument is also not shown to be equivalent to the stated SICP process.

The signed-weight and robustness results do not repair these problems. Condition 4.3 introduces unspecified instance-dependent constants that can make the bound vacuous, and several proof inequalities and index manipulations are unjustified. Theorem 4.5 assumes an absolute multiplicative approximation for every subset even when sigma may be zero or negative; this neither preserves signs nor supports the ordering used in its proof. No sampling result establishes the premise.

A-CauIM has no approximation guarantee and its heuristic is questionable. The alleged hyperedge probability in Equation 4 can exceed one. Equation 5 weights a local derivative by a candidate's current activation probability, potentially assigning zero score to a disconnected but excellent new seed while favoring nodes already likely to activate. This is not the discrete marginal gain.

The empirical validation is circular and largely semi-synthetic. The three 'real-world' datasets principally supply graph structures, while causal treatments, outcomes, covariates, or ITEs are simulated without a complete data-generating specification. Seed sets are evaluated using the same estimated ITE model that guides selection, rather than true counterfactual policy value or an oracle, so the experiments do not validate causal recovery or real-world utility.

Only random selection and a vaguely specified greedy baseline are compared; competitive hypergraph IM, dynamic/weighted IM, causal-policy, and exact-oracle baselines are absent. Results have no uncertainty intervals. A-CauIM underperforms the baseline on Contact and barely improves it on GoodReads, while G-CauIM is slower than the baseline, yet the discussion claims broad superiority. The noise experiment measures output variance rather than value or regret and does not test the theorem's error model.

Reproducibility and clarity are poor: Algorithm 1 contains an ill-defined parameter update; several variables and seed-set symbols are undefined or inconsistent; essential architecture, optimization, hyperparameter, graph-size, hardware, outcome-generation, and stopping details are missing. Reported Torch versions, iteration counts, figure dataset labels, and the runtime-table caption conflict. Training and estimator costs are excluded from the complexity and timing comparison.

The relationship to prior work does not establish substantial originality beyond combining an existing hypergraph treatment-effect representation with weighted greedy selection and an autograd heuristic. The paper also lacks a candid discussion of estimator misspecification, interference assumptions, approximation bias, and fairness/privacy concerns in its targeted-marketing and HIV-awareness examples. Because the causal estimand, influence calculation, principal guarantees, and evaluation are all materially unsupported, the deficiencies are fundamental and warrant a Strong Reject.

strengths: The paper addresses an important limitation of conventional influence maximization: node utility may depend on counterfactual outcomes and changing network exposure. Combining interference-aware treatment-effect estimation with hypergraph seed selection is potentially useful and original. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/neurips2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-2c9h00kx/call-95db8a3ddddd4f1cba259cabc94710c0/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The paper proposes both a simulation-based method and a faster differentiable surrogate, and attempts to analyze signed utilities and estimation error rather than assuming all node weights are positive.

The appendix includes proof attempts, algorithm pseudocode, public-data references, and an anonymous implementation link. Experiments span several distinct hypergraph structures and report both objective values and runtime.
No actual human intervention is reported, and most outcomes appear simulated, so there is no evident unresolved severe ethical issue.
weaknesses: The causal formulation is not identified. Assumption 2.2 states that the two potential outcomes are conditionally independent of each other, whereas identification requires an appropriate independence between treatment assignment and potential outcomes, together with positivity and a justified exposure mapping. Consistency alone does not recover the missing counterfactuals. Moreover, summing local ITEs under interference is not shown to equal a well-defined causal contrast between seeding policies.

The objective is internally inconsistent. The activation probability is defined as a sum of single-source reachability probabilities, which double-counts overlapping paths and can exceed one. Since each ITE depends on the realized activation environment and hence on the seed set, multiplying a marginal activation probability by that random ITE does not generally yield the expected realized gain.

The main approximation theorem effectively treats ITEs as fixed weights. Even if every realized ITE is positive, seed-dependent environmental changes can destroy monotonicity and submodularity. The appendix further relies on an expression that sums reachability separately over seeds and therefore double-counts influence. With negative ITEs, the algorithm forces exactly K seeds although the stated constraint permits fewer, while the additive bound can be vacuous.

The robustness theorem assumes a uniform multiplicative approximation for every seed set without deriving it from Monte Carlo sampling or ITE-estimation error. Such ratios are undefined when the objective is zero and problematic when it is negative. The corollary adds another unverified condition rather than establishing sample complexity or estimator robustness.

A-CauIM is an unsupported heuristic, not an approximation to the discrete greedy marginal established by analysis. Its hyperedge quantity labeled a probability can exceed one; the activation-to-treatment transform is not guaranteed to lie in [0,1]; and the derivative score can favor nodes already likely to activate rather than nodes with high incremental seed value. No guarantee connects A-CauIM to the theory, and its complexity omits fixed-point iterations, autodifferentiation, and ITE-estimation costs.

G-CauIM is not executable from the specification: its post-training parameter update contains undefined quantities and an ill-posed optimization, the balancing penalty and architecture are omitted, and enforcing a bound on predictions does not justify extrapolation to unseen network exposures.

The empirical evidence is insufficient and partly circular. The three “real-world” datasets supply network structures, while treatments, covariates, and causal outcomes appear simulated; the outcome-generating process and true ITEs are not specified. Seed sets are evaluated using the same learned ITE module used for selection, with no independent ground truth, policy-value estimator, PEHE analysis, or oracle comparison.

Baselines are limited to unweighted greedy and random selection; relevant weighted-IM, hypergraph-IM, causal-estimation, static-ITE, and nonmonotone optimization alternatives are absent. Results lack uncertainties or significance tests despite repeated trials, A-CauIM underperforms greedy on Contact, and the noise experiment plots variance rather than policy regret or recovery accuracy.

Reproducibility and clarity are poor despite the code link: dataset sizes, preprocessing, outcome simulation, splits, model hyperparameters, convergence criteria, hardware, and random seeds are missing. Torch versions conflict across sections, captions and algorithm numbering are inconsistent, and notation changes between O/Q, f/σ, and k/K. The visible authorship/arXiv watermark and overlength main text also appear incompatible with a double-blind NeurIPS submission. These foundational technical and evaluation deficiencies make the central claims unsupported.

strengths: The manuscript targets an important problem: influence-maximization utilities may be heterogeneous, unobserved, and affected by network interference. Connecting this issue to causal effect estimation is conceptually interesting.

The authors attempt an end-to-end framework spanning hypergraph diffusion, interference-aware ITE estimation, greedy optimization, and a faster differentiable approximation. Considering negative and environment-dependent gains is more ambitious than standard fixed-weight IM.

The evaluation includes four network structures, runtime comparisons, and noise and propagation-parameter analyses. The reported acceleration of A-CauIM could be practically valuable if established rigorously.
weaknesses: The central formulation is internally inconsistent. The ITE is defined as depending on propagation-dependent treatment states and hence on the seed set and cascade, but the theoretical analysis treats each ITE as a fixed node weight. Moreover, multiplying an activation probability by a state-dependent ITE does not generally equal expected realized utility because the quantities are correlated. Consequently, positivity of the ITE does not establish monotonicity or submodularity, and Theorem 4.4 does not apply to the environmentally sensitive problem being claimed.

The causal identification argument is incorrect. Assumption 2.2 states that the two potential outcomes are mutually independent conditional on treatment and environment; causal identification instead requires treatment assignment to be independent of the potential-outcome vector conditional on adequate pre-treatment variables, together with positivity and a well-defined interference exposure mapping. These conditions are neither stated nor justified, so the counterfactual ITEs are not identified from the observational data described.

Several identities underpinning the proofs are unsupported or false for general cascade models. In particular, writing an activation probability as a sum of reachability probabilities from individual seeds and Equation 7's additive decomposition double-count overlapping paths and seed influence and may exceed one. The subsequent marginal-gain and approximation arguments therefore do not follow.

The negative-ITE and robustness results are not meaningful as stated. The multiplicative condition on estimated versus true influence is undefined at zero and does not support the proof's inequalities for negative objectives. It is assumed uniformly over all seed sets without a sample-complexity or probability result. The epsilon-dependent lower bound can also be negative and vacuous, while the appendix contains undefined symbols, inconsistent indices, and unjustified algebraic transitions.

A-CauIM is an unsupported heuristic rather than a demonstrated acceleration of greedy CauIM. Its probability recursion is not derived from SICP and can assign a quantity called a hyperedge probability a value above one. The derivative with respect to a node's current activation probability is not the discrete marginal effect of adding that node as a seed. No approximation guarantee or controlled fidelity experiment connects this rule to G-CauIM.

The empirical evaluation cannot validate the causal claims. Only the network structures are real; treatments, covariates, outcomes, and ITEs are simulated or incompletely described. Performance is evaluated using the same learned ITE module used for optimization, creating a circular metric, with no assessment against ground-truth effects, realized outcomes, or an oracle policy.

Baselines are inadequate: the paper compares primarily against unweighted greedy selection and random choice, but omits the essential fixed-weight learned-ITE greedy baseline, alternative interference estimators, weighted IM methods, and scalable IM algorithms. There are no uncertainty intervals or statistical tests. A-CauIM is worse than the baseline on Contact, contrary to the broad improvement claim, and the robustness plot measures output variance rather than regret or degradation required by the theorem.

Reproducibility is inadequate in the reviewed manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/neurips2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-gkvfyyrv/call-35e6d0ea588f4743ba7734bdf2e335d7/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}. It omits dataset sizes, the outcome/ITE simulator, estimator architecture, optimization settings, key constants, diffusion stopping criteria, and complete hardware details; reported Torch versions are inconsistent. Algorithm 1 also contains undefined variables and an ill-defined parameter-update operation.

Clarity is substantially impaired by inconsistent objectives and notation, mislabeled algorithm references and figure captions, contradictory runtime captions, very small plots, and pervasive grammatical errors. The relationship to adaptive or dynamic-weight IM, causal policy learning under interference, and network welfare optimization is also too limited to establish the claimed novelty. Ethical implications of targeting individuals in health and social-network applications, including privacy and fairness, are not discussed.

strengths: The paper identifies a potentially important limitation of weighted influence maximization: node utility may depend on the evolving activation state of its neighborhood. Connecting this problem to causal inference under network interference is an interesting direction.
Considering hypergraphs, signed gains, and both accuracy-oriented and accelerated algorithms could be useful if formulated rigorously.
The manuscript includes intuitive diagrams, attempted theoretical analysis, experiments on four graph topologies, and preliminary runtime, noise, and propagation-probability studies.
weaknesses: The central causal identification claim is invalid. Assumption 2.2 asserts independence between the two potential outcomes conditional on treatment and environment, rather than exchangeability between treatment and potential outcomes, and no positivity assumption is given. Consequently, the stated identification equality does not follow. Recovering counterfactual node-level effects from one factual outcome per node is especially unjustified under interference and dynamically endogenous activation.

The proposed objective does not correctly represent the joint cascade. Since the treatment effect depends on the random surrounding activation state, expected realized gain generally cannot be factored into activation probability times expected treatment effect. It also neglects feedback and spillover effects induced by changing a node's activation.

The theoretical analysis studies a different, fixed-weight problem from the environmentally dynamic problem motivating the paper. It treats each τ as independent of the seed set and cascade state. Moreover, the identity ap(v;S)=sum over seeds of their individual reachability probabilities is generally false because reachability events overlap; Equation 7 therefore double-counts nodes. This invalidates the main approximation analysis.

The signed-weight guarantees are not sound or meaningful. The algorithm always selects exactly K seeds although the formulation permits at most K, which matters without monotonicity. The multiplicative robustness condition is undefined at zero and invalid for negative objective values, while its constants can make the lower bound vacuous. Several proof steps also assume unjustified independence of reachability events and use inconsistent notation.

A-CauIM has no guarantee connecting its derivative score to the discrete marginal gain. Equation 5 scores a candidate using its activation probability under the current seed set; with an empty seed set all such probabilities are zero, and valuable currently unreachable candidates can continue to receive zero score. The probability recursion is an unsupported mean-field approximation that can violate probability semantics and omits initialization and convergence details.

G-CauIM is not reproducibly specified: its parameter perturbation is undefined, its boundedness constraint is one-sided despite the absolute-value assumption, and the procedure changes model parameters after treatment configurations change without new outcomes. A-CauIM similarly lacks complete pseudocode and essential constants, architecture, training, and stopping details.

The empirical evaluation is largely circular: seed selection and evaluation both use effects produced by the same learned ITE model, with no validation against true counterfactual effects or realized policy outcomes. The nominally real-world datasets mainly supply graph structures while treatments, covariates, and effects are simulated or insufficiently described.

Only unweighted greedy and random selection are compared; there is no static weighted-IM baseline, causal policy-learning baseline, oracle, or small-instance optimum. Reported improvements are often small, A-CauIM is worse than the baseline on Contact, and no uncertainty or significance estimates are supplied despite multiple runs. The noise experiment does not match the theorem's uniform multiplicative-error assumption.

Numerous inconsistencies further impede assessment, including mismatched figure captions, contradictory Torch versions, missing dataset statistics and outcome-generation equations, and exaggerated real-world and robustness conclusions. The sensitive HIV-awareness motivation also lacks discussion of fairness, privacy, or deployment limitations. Together with the fundamental identification and proof failures, these issues rule out acceptance.

strengths: The paper targets an important limitation of standard influence maximization: utilities may be heterogeneous, counterfactual, affected by network interference, and sometimes negative. Connecting this setting to causal-effect estimation is potentially valuable and original.
The proposed framework is ambitious, combining hypergraph diffusion, an interference-aware outcome model, greedy seed selection, and a faster differentiable approximation.

The manuscript includes algorithm descriptions, attempted approximation and robustness analyses, appendix proofs, experiments on three real network topologies plus a synthetic graph, runtime measurements, and an anonymous code link.
The experiments are simulation-based on public network structures, so no immediate human-subject or serious ethical issue is apparent.
weaknesses: The causal estimand is not adequately defined or identified. The notation conflates treatment/recommendation with activation produced by diffusion, while the environmental representation contains downstream activation states. Assumption 2.2 states independence between potential outcomes rather than conditional exchangeability with treatment, and positivity and exposure-mapping assumptions are absent. Consequently, individual treatment effects cannot generally be recovered from one factual outcome per node as claimed.

The main approximation theorem is incompatible with the paper's central premise. Its proof treats each tau_i as a fixed node weight, although tau_i is defined to change with the seed-dependent activation environment. Even if every realized tau_i is positive, adding a seed can reduce existing nodes' positive utilities enough to destroy monotonicity and submodularity, so the claimed 1-1/e guarantee does not follow.

The influence objective itself uses an invalid reachability identity: ap(v;S) is written as a sum of per-seed reachability probabilities, which double-counts overlapping cascades and can exceed one. Equation 7 inherits this problem, undermining the subsequent claims and proofs.

The negative-effect and robustness results have additional serious gaps. Condition 4.3 is ambiguous and can yield a vacuous additive bound; several proof inequalities and indices are inconsistent; and the uniform multiplicative assumption on estimated influence is undefined or unusable when the signed objective is zero or negative. No sampling complexity or probabilistic guarantee connects this assumption to the Monte Carlo procedure.

A-CauIM is an unsupported heuristic rather than a justified acceleration of greedy CauIM. The quantity called a hyperedge activation probability in Equation 4 can exceed one and does not clearly preserve cumulative, absorbing infection dynamics. The derivative-times-current-probability score is not the marginal benefit of adding a seed; with an empty seed set, all current activation probabilities can be zero, leaving the first selection indeterminate. No approximation or error bound is provided for A-CauIM, and its complexity omits convergence iterations and ITE estimation.

The evaluation does not validate the causal component. The supposedly real-world experiments use real graph structures but simulated treatments, covariates, and outcomes; the generative mechanism is incompletely specified, and the metric appears to reuse the same learned ITE model used for optimization. There is no held-out counterfactual evaluation, PEHE/regret measurement, oracle comparison, or test of whether environmental effects are recovered.

The empirical comparison is too weak for the claims: only unweighted greedy and random selection are used, uncertainty and significance are omitted, A-CauIM underperforms the baseline on one dataset, and the noise experiment does not test the theorem's assumptions. Runtime results lack graph sizes, hardware details, convergence criteria, scaling studies, and a controlled quality-runtime comparison.

Reproducibility is inadequate despite the code link. Essential details such as preprocessing, complete outcome simulation, network architecture, balancing loss, optimizer, train/test protocol, C, Cd, M, propagation convergence, and random seeds are missing. Numerous notation inconsistencies and grammatical errors further obscure the method. The paper also lacks a substantive limitations discussion and does not address privacy, fairness, or intervention harms relevant to its targeting and public-health examples. These are fundamental deficiencies in the central theory and validation, not issues addressable by minor revision.

strengths: The manuscript tackles a meaningful limitation of conventional influence maximization: utilities may be heterogeneous, negative, and dependent on neighboring activation states. Connecting network interference, causal-effect estimation, and hypergraph influence maximization is potentially valuable. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/neurips2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-vhhw2uq6/call-9ae57444409444c08fa1bdf9f11cfe61/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The paper attempts a broad contribution comprising a formal objective, a simulation-based greedy method, a differentiable accelerated method, approximation analysis, and empirical evaluation on multiple network topologies.
The reported runtime reduction for A-CauIM is potentially significant, and explicitly considering negative effects, estimator noise, and interference is directionally useful.
weaknesses: The causal identification argument is fundamentally incorrect or incomplete. Assumption 2.2 states that the two potential outcomes are mutually independent conditional on treatment and environment; this is not treatment ignorability. Identification instead requires suitable independence between treatment assignment and potential outcomes, positivity, consistency for the full exposure mapping, and treatment-allocation assumptions. These are absent, while the neighborhood activation variables are themselves post-seeding and endogenous. Consequently, the learned conditional outcome difference cannot generally be interpreted as an individual treatment effect.

The mathematical objective is inconsistent with network diffusion. The equality ap(v;S)=sum_{u in S} pr(u,v) generally double-counts overlapping paths and influence from multiple seeds, invalidating Equation 7 and the subsequent proofs. Moreover, because tau_i depends on the realized neighboring activation state, E[A_i tau_i(T_-i)] cannot generally be factored into an activation probability times an unconditional expected tau_i. The algorithms emphasize dynamic effects, whereas the theory treats tau_i as fixed.

The claimed guarantees are not established for the stated problem. Negative utilities destroy monotonicity and nonnegativity, make multiplicative error assumptions undefined when sigma is zero or negative, and conflict with an algorithm that always selects exactly K seeds although the optimization permits at most K. Condition 4.3 can yield arbitrarily large, vacuous constants, and its one-node probability bound is used for sets differing by multiple nodes. There are also notation, sign, and recurrence errors in the appendix. No guarantee covers A-CauIM's approximations.

Both algorithms are underspecified. G-CauIM's parameter-perturbation rule is not operationally defined and its constraint bounds tau only on one side. A-CauIM's mean-field probability recursion lacks an error analysis, its exponential treatment transformation as written does not map into the claimed binary-like range, and its derivative score measures local sensitivity rather than the finite marginal gain from making a node a seed. The complexity claim excludes estimator cost and convergence iterations.

The empirical evaluation cannot validate the causal claims. The three so-called real-world experiments use real network topology but simulated covariates, treatments, outcomes, or ITEs. Seed sets are evaluated using the same learned ITE module used for optimization, creating a circular metric. The paper reports neither ground-truth treatment-effect error nor true policy utility, and it does not compare against an oracle optimum even on the 100-node synthetic case.

Baselines and reporting are inadequate. Only a vaguely specified traditional greedy method and random selection are central comparisons; relevant static weighted-IM, causal-policy, interference-aware, heuristic, and sketch-based alternatives are missing. A-CauIM is worse than the baseline on Contact, and random selection exceeds the baseline on SD-100, contradicting broad superiority claims. No error bars or statistical tests are reported, and high-noise results are explicitly omitted because they increase sharply.

Reproducibility is poor despite the code link. Essential details are missing, including graph statistics, complete outcome/ITE generation equations, train/validation/test construction, architecture and optimizer settings, the balancing penalty, C and C_d, simulation budgets, and hardware. PyTorch versions, figure captions, algorithm numbering, and the runtime-table caption are inconsistent.

The relationship to prior work does not adequately establish originality beyond combining an existing hypergraph causal estimator with weighted influence maximization. The school-contact/HIV-awareness example also warrants discussion of privacy, fairness, stigmatization, and responsible targeting, although no actual human intervention is reported. Overall, the invalid causal identification and objective/theory mismatch are foundational deficiencies rather than minor experimental omissions.

strengths: The manuscript identifies a meaningful problem: influence-maximization utilities may be unobservable, heterogeneous, and dependent on neighboring activation states. Connecting this issue to causal inference under interference is potentially valuable. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/neurips2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-c_2isq5a/call-50703c7a9cb24df9ad100b02749499a7/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
Considering hypergraphs, negative utilities, and changing node-level gains is broader than standard nonnegative weighted influence maximization.
The paper attempts a comprehensive contribution, including greedy and accelerated algorithms, approximation and robustness analyses, several datasets, runtime measurements, code, and appendices.
weaknesses: The causal identification argument is fundamentally inadequate. Assumption 2.2 states independence between potential outcomes conditional on treatment and environment, rather than ignorability of treatment assignment given pre-treatment covariates; positivity is also absent. A neural network trained only on factual outcomes cannot identify individual counterfactual effects without substantially stronger assumptions or experimental structure.

The objective is not coherently derived from the potential-outcomes setup. Activation is simultaneously treated as treatment, diffusion state, and a probability multiplier. Moreover, ap(v;S)=sum_{u in S} pr(u,v) is generally false because reachability events overlap and the sum can exceed one. Equation 7 consequently does not represent standard cascade probability and appears to double-count seeds.

The central theoretical result does not cover the stated problem. Although the paper emphasizes that tau_i changes with the seed set and propagation environment, the proofs treat every tau_i as a fixed node weight. Nonnegative but seed-dependent utilities need not yield a monotone submodular objective. Thus even the positive-weight guarantee does not justify G-CauIM as described.

The negative-weight proof contains unsupported equalities and sign/bounding issues, while Condition 4.3 can yield a vacuous lower bound. The robustness theorem merely assumes uniform relative accuracy over every subset, which is especially ill-defined when the objective may be zero or negative; it provides neither a Monte Carlo sample bound nor a valid connection to the proposed ITE estimator.

A-CauIM is an unvalidated heuristic. Equation 4 does not correctly account for correlated cascade events and can produce invalid intermediate hyperedge probabilities, while the derivative score in Equation 5 is not the discrete marginal gain from adding a seed. No theorem or approximation-error analysis links A-CauIM to either G-CauIM or the proposed objective.

The empirical evaluation is largely circular. The datasets provide graph structure, but treatments, covariates, and effects are simulated or insufficiently specified, and performance is measured using the same learned ITE estimator that guides seed selection. There is no evaluation against true causal utility, oracle effects, held-out outcomes, PEHE, or policy value.

The baselines and statistical evidence are inadequate. Only traditional greedy and random selection are reported; relevant weighted, hypergraph, sketch-based, and causal-policy methods are omitted. There are no confidence intervals or significance tests, and A-CauIM is worse than the baseline on Contact despite the broad superiority claims.

The robustness experiment measures variability after injecting noise rather than degradation relative to true utility, and it is not connected quantitatively to the theorem's parameters. RQ3 promises component analysis but only varies the diffusion probability; essential choices such as the interference encoder, parameter adjustment, smoothing constants, and gradient proxy are not ablated.

Reproducibility is insufficient from the manuscript: the outcome-generation mechanism, dataset sizes and preprocessing, model architecture, optimization details, constants C, C_d, and M, convergence criteria, and precise hardware are missing. The reported Torch versions are inconsistent, and the runtime comparison excludes important costs.

Presentation problems further obscure verification: Algorithm 1's parameter perturbation is not operationally defined, notation changes meaning across sections, several captions name the wrong method or dataset, and numerous mathematical and linguistic errors remain. The paper also lacks a substantive limitations or responsible-use discussion for behavioral and health-related targeting scenarios.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/neurips2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-2_muqymn/call-24df016d990646ef9cf58bdc75fce67e/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses a meaningful limitation of conventional influence maximization: individual utility may be unobservable, affected by network interference, and change during diffusion. This is a potentially useful problem direction.

The paper attempts an ambitious end-to-end treatment, including a causal estimator, a greedy method, an accelerated heuristic, approximation and robustness analyses, and experiments on several hypergraph structures.

The acceleration goal is practically relevant because simulation-based greedy influence maximization is expensive; the reported runtimes suggest potentially substantial savings if the approximation can be validated.

The diagrams convey the intended pipeline reasonably well, a code link is supplied, and no unresolved material ethical issue is evident because the reported outcomes and interventions appear simulated. Deployment in advertising or health settings would nevertheless require privacy, consent, and fairness analysis.
weaknesses: The central mathematical formulation is internally inconsistent. The assertion ap(i;S) = sum over seeds u of pr(u,i) ignores overlapping reachability events and can exceed one. Equation 7 repeats this additive decomposition and may also count seed utility twice. With fixed node effects it makes the objective modular, conflicting with the claimed NP-hard optimization and submodular-greedy analysis.

The theory omits the paper's main novelty. The treatment effects are claimed to change with the seed set and cascade environment, but the proofs treat every tau_i as a fixed weight. Positivity of dynamically changing weights does not imply monotonicity or submodularity: adding a seed can reduce existing nodes' positive effects enough to lower the objective. Consequently, Theorem 4.4 does not establish the claimed guarantee for either implemented method.

The proofs contain further substantive gaps. Condition 4.3 bounds changes between sets differing by one node, but Equation 9 and Claims 2-3 apply the same epsilon bound to arbitrary nested sets. The negative-effect setting also permits zero or negative objectives, making the multiplicative relative-error premise and positivity-based inequalities in Theorem 4.5 invalid. Several expressions use undefined f, inconsistent indices, or unexplained algebra, and the resulting additive-error bound can be vacuous.

Causal identification is not established. Assumption 2.2 is written as independence between the two potential outcomes rather than ignorability of treatment given covariates and exposure; positivity and support conditions are absent. The exposure mapping ENV is unspecified, and the manuscript does not explain how the observational regime supplies enough variation to recover counterfactual effects under interference. The learned quantity is at best a model-dependent conditional effect, not an identified individual treatment effect under the stated assumptions.

Algorithm 1 is not operationally defined: the parameter perturbation in line 12 contains undefined variables and no optimization objective, while its one-sided constraint does not enforce the assumed absolute bound. Important parts of the balancing loss, architecture, and dynamic updates are omitted.

A-CauIM is an unsupported heuristic. Its hyperedge recurrence is a mean-field expression rather than a valid activation-probability calculation and can assign a hyperedge quantity above one. The derivative-times-current-activation score is not the discrete marginal gain; in particular, at an empty seed set all current activation probabilities are zero, so the stated rule cannot select a first seed. No approximation error or theoretical guarantee connects this procedure to the CauIM objective.

The experiments do not validate the causal or real-world claims. The datasets provide real graph structures, but treatments, covariates, and outcomes appear simulated, with the outcome generator largely delegated to a citation. Seed selection and evaluation use the same estimated ITE model, creating a circular metric; there is no held-out factual-outcome evaluation, ground-truth counterfactual error, oracle regret, or comparison against known true effects.

The baseline set is inadequate: only unweighted greedy and random selection are emphasized, with no competitive weighted-IM, static-effect, causal-policy, or interference-aware alternatives. There are no error bars or statistical tests, A-CauIM is worse than the baseline on Contact, and the noise experiment reports output variance rather than degradation relative to an oracle or satisfaction of Theorem 4.5's assumptions.

Reproducibility is insufficient despite the code link. Missing information includes dataset sizes and preprocessing, complete synthetic outcome equations, train/validation splits, network architecture, optimizer and training schedule, balancing coefficient, C, Cd, M, r0, hardware, and exact simulation settings. The manuscript also conflicts on 20 versus 50 diffusion rounds and Torch 1.11 versus 2.1, and Figure 3 labels Email-Eu as Contact.

The originality is not convincingly isolated from combining an existing hypergraph treatment-effect estimator with weighted greedy influence maximization. The relationship to dynamic-weight influence maximization and intervention-policy optimization under network interference is too limited, and the empirical comparisons do not establish an advantage over those closest alternatives. These fundamental formulation, proof, and validation deficiencies determine the strong-reject recommendation.

strengths: The paper identifies a potentially important extension of influence maximization: node gains may be heterogeneous, negative, counterfactual, and dependent on neighboring activation states.

Combining network-interference modeling, hypergraph diffusion, and seed selection is conceptually interesting. Providing both a simulation-based method and a faster differentiable approximation is a useful design ambition.
The manuscript includes attempted approximation and robustness analyses, experiments on four graph structures, runtime measurements, appendices, and an implementation link.
weaknesses: The causal estimand is not identified by the stated assumptions. Assumption 2.2 incorrectly makes the two potential outcomes independent of each other, whereas identification requires conditions relating treatment assignment to potential outcomes, along with positivity and a justified exposure mapping. Activation is also treated simultaneously as an endogenous diffusion outcome and as treatment. Consequently, one observed outcome per node cannot generally identify the claimed individual treatment effects under interference; the network model would at best estimate conditional average effects under substantial additional assumptions.

The optimization objective is mathematically inconsistent. The claimed identity ap(v_i;S)=sum_{u in S} pr(u,v_i) double-counts overlapping reachability events and can exceed one. Moreover, multiplying an unconditional activation probability by a treatment effect that depends on the same realized cascade does not equal the expected realized gain without an appropriate conditional expectation.

The main theoretical guarantee does not cover the proposed setting. Theorem 4.4 treats each tau_i as a fixed node weight, while the central premise is that tau_i changes with the seed set and cascade environment. Even strictly positive state-dependent weights need not produce a monotone or submodular objective, so the stated 1-1/e result does not follow. Equation 7 also assumes additivity across seeds and hence inherits the reachability double-counting error.

The negative-weight and robustness analyses contain additional serious problems. Condition 4.3 is essentially satisfiable using large, potentially vacuous constants; Appendix F appears to collapse an accumulated O(K epsilon_2) error into an O(epsilon_2) term; and the multiplicative-error assumption in Theorem 4.5 is undefined when sigma(S) is zero and invalidly handled when it is negative. No Monte Carlo sample complexity is given to establish this assumed uniform error.

A-CauIM is neither sufficiently specified nor justified as an accelerated greedy method. Its activation recurrence is not derived as an exact probability recurrence for SICP, the continuous treatment transformation and constants C and C_d are unexplained, and evaluating a nonlinear ITE model at mean activation probabilities does not generally estimate expected ITE. Most importantly, the score derivative times ap(v;S) is not the marginal effect of making v a seed: all scores vanish when S is empty, and the rule can favor already-reachable, redundant nodes. No approximation result is proved for A-CauIM.

The empirical evidence does not validate the causal or optimization claims. The supposedly real-world experiments use real graph structures but simulated treatments, covariates, and outcomes; the outcome-generating equations are omitted. Performance is evaluated using the same learned ITE module used for optimization, without oracle causal outcomes, policy value estimation, or a small-instance optimal solution. Comparisons are limited to random selection and an underspecified greedy baseline, omitting relevant weighted-IM and causal-effect baselines.

Results are overstated and statistically unsupported. A-CauIM is worse than the baseline on Contact, several gains are modest, and no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported despite repeated trials. The robustness study reports variability rather than value loss or regret, uses one dataset, and does not measure the quantities in the theorem. Runtime comparisons conflate Monte Carlo optimization with a different deterministic surrogate and omit adequate hardware and accuracy-versus-runtime controls.

Reproducibility and clarity are inadequate: graph sizes, complete simulation mechanisms, model architecture, training protocol, balancing loss, parameter-update rule, convergence criteria, and key hyperparameters are absent. Algorithms contain undefined expressions, and there are conflicting captions, dataset names, software versions, equation signs, and algorithm references. If submitted unchanged to a double-blind venue, the displayed author identities, affiliations, emails, and arXiv identifier are also problematic. The sensitive HIV-intervention example receives no discussion of fairness, consent, or harms.

strengths: The paper targets an important, insufficiently explored problem: influence maximization when node utilities are heterogeneous, counterfactual, and affected by network interference.

Combining causal-effect estimation with hypergraph influence maximization is potentially useful, and considering negative as well as positive individual effects is more realistic than standard nonnegative weighted-IM formulations.
The authors attempt an end-to-end treatment encompassing modeling, a greedy method, an accelerated approximation, theoretical analysis, and experiments on several network structures.
The intuitive examples and diagrams communicate the motivating idea reasonably well, and an implementation link is provided.
weaknesses: The causal objective is not coherently justified. The desired cascade value should involve the joint quantity E[I_i tau_i(T_-i)], whereas the paper multiplies the marginal activation probability by an environment-dependent treatment effect, effectively ignoring their dependence. Under interference, summing conditional individual effects also does not generally equal the value of a joint intervention without additional additivity assumptions.

The identification assumptions are inadequate and partly misstated. Assumption 2.2 asserts independence between potential outcomes rather than conditional ignorability of treatment; positivity is absent, and a single observational network realization does not identify counterfactual outcomes under new cascade environments merely through a representation model.

The main theoretical results do not analyze the proposed dynamic-ITE setting. Their proofs treat tau_i as a fixed node weight, even though the central premise and algorithms make it change with the seed-induced environment. Positive but seed-dependent weights need not yield a monotone or submodular objective.

The proof also relies on incorrect influence identities. In general, ap(v;S) is not the sum of pairwise reachability probabilities from all seeds because their reachability events overlap; Equation 7 consequently double-counts activations. Later marginal-gain factorizations are likewise not valid for a general IC/SICP cascade. Approximation ratios and multiplicative robustness bounds are additionally ill-defined when the objective can be zero or negative.

A-CauIM is an unsupported heuristic rather than an accelerated implementation of greedy selection. Its probability recurrence is not derived for a progressive cascade, may not compute eventual activation probabilities, and omits convergence cost. The proposed gradient-times-current-probability score is not a discrete seed marginal gain; notably, it assigns zero score to an unreached node with activation probability zero even though seeding that node may be highly valuable. No approximation guarantee is established for A-CauIM.

G-CauIM is not operationally specified. The per-cascade parameter perturbation in Algorithm 1 is undefined, changing trained parameters conflicts with treating the outcome model as invariant, and the stated constraint bounds only tau_i from above rather than bounding its absolute value. A-CauIM lacks complete pseudocode and many implementation details.

The empirical evaluation cannot substantiate the causal or optimization claims. Network topologies are real, but outcomes, covariates, and ITEs appear simulated; the reported policy value is computed with the same learned ITE estimator used for seed selection, rather than ground-truth or held-out outcomes. There is no ITE-estimation metric, oracle optimum on small instances, or evaluation of actual intervention value.

Baselines are limited to random and an ambiguous traditional greedy method, omitting relevant weighted/hypergraph IM methods and causal policy-learning approaches. Results have no error bars or significance tests, improvements are small or negative in some cases, and the noise study evaluates A-CauIM even though the theorem concerns noisy greedy evaluation and its assumptions are never checked.

Reproducibility is inadequate despite the code link: dataset sizes and preprocessing, outcome-generation equations, treatment rates, model architecture, optimizer and training protocol, constants C, Cd, M and r0, hardware, and convergence criteria are missing. Iteration counts and Torch versions are inconsistent, and several table captions and dataset labels are erroneous.

The paper lacks a candid limitations and ethics discussion. This is particularly relevant when motivating targeting policies for health-awareness interventions, where confounding, privacy, unequal allocation, and harms from erroneous causal estimates matter.

Please serve as an expert reviewer for the NeurIPS 2025 main research track.
Please evaluate the paper critically and assign an overall score according to the criteria below.

Assess technical quality, clarity, significance, and originality. Check whether the work is sufficiently complete, whether its claims are supported by appropriate theory or experiments, and whether its relationship to prior knowledge is clearly established. Consider whether the contribution provides useful knowledge or capabilities for the relevant research community.

Judge reproducibility and research ethics in relation to the actual claims and evidence. Recognize original insights as well as new methods. An explicit and honest discussion of limitations is useful information, not an automatic reason for a lower score. Explain which strengths and weaknesses determine the recommendation.

Assign an Overall Assessment (OA) score using only: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, or 6.

Rating scale:
1 = Strong Reject
Fundamental deficiencies, a lack of substantive new contribution, or unresolved serious ethical issues rule out acceptance.

2 = Reject
Important shortcomings in technical support, evaluation, or reproducibility outweigh the paper's merits.

3 = Borderline reject
The work is technically solid but the reasons against acceptance slightly outweigh those in favor. Please use sparingly.

4 = Borderline accept
The work is technically solid and the reasons for acceptance slightly outweigh the remaining concerns. Please use sparingly.

5 = Accept
The paper offers a strong, well-supported contribution with meaningful impact and adequate reproducibility.

6 = Strong Accept
The work offers an exceptional and potentially field-changing contribution, with outstanding technical support and no unresolved material ethical concerns.

attempts.raw_response: {"oa":1,"strengths":["The manuscript studies an important and potentially original problem: influence maximization when node utilities are heterogeneous, counterfactual, and sensitive to neighboring activation states, connecting network causal inference with hypergraph optimization. :codex-file-citation{path=\"/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/neurips2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-cglajmv5/call-07d129efae78459ca76c55863c9e3936/manuscript.pdf\" purpose=\"source\"}","It presents both a simulation-based greedy method and a substantially faster vectorized heuristic, reflecting a useful accuracy-efficiency design goal.","The authors attempt to address difficult cases involving negative treatment effects and noisy effect estimates, rather than restricting attention to conventional fixed, nonnegative node weights.","The evaluation uses several graph structures and reports runtime, noise, and propagation-probability sensitivity; appendices and an anonymous code link also show some attention to reproducibility."],"weaknesses":["The causal objective is not correctly derived. Because tau_i depends on the realized neighboring treatment vector, the expected activated gain is E[1{T_i=1} tau_i(T_-i)], not ap(i;S)E[tau_i] without a conditional-independence argument. More generally, summing own-treatment contrasts does not equal the total policy effect under interference, which should compare aggregate potential outcomes under two treatment vectors. Thus the optimized quantity is not convincingly connected to the claimed profit or intervention benefit.","Identification is unsupported. Assumption 2.2 is written as independence between the two potential outcomes conditional on treatment and environment, rather than ignorability of treatment given pre-treatment covariates. Positivity, a valid exposure mapping, and support for environmental states induced by new seed policies are absent. A single factual outcome per node plus an HGCN does not by itself identify individual counterfactual effects, especially under network dependence and policy-induced distribution shift.","A central influence calculation is incorrect: ap(v;S) is defined as the sum of single-seed reachability probabilities, although reachability events from different seeds overlap and their probabilities cannot generally be added. Equation 7 repeats this additive decomposition and can double-count activated nodes. The subsequent approximation proof therefore does not apply to the stated diffusion model.","The theory analyzes fixed node weights, contradicting the paper's defining premise that treatment effects change with the environment and seed set. Even positive environment-dependent weights need not yield a submodular objective. The negative-weight bound relies on the erroneous fixed-weight decomposition, contains unjustified inequalities, can be vacuous through its unrestricted additive epsilon terms, and is inconsistent with the formulation allowing at most K seeds while the algorithm forces exactly K despite potentially negative marginal gains.","The robustness theorem uses multiplicative ratios involving sigma(S), which may be zero or negative in the setting explicitly emphasized by the paper; several inequality directions then cease to be valid. Its uniform relative-error premise is not linked to the pointwise ITE-error condition, and the Gaussian-noise experiment measures variance rather than regret against an oracle, so it does not validate the theorem.","A-CauIM is an unsupported heuristic rather than an accelerated implementation of greedy selection. The score (d sigma/d ap(v;S)) ap(v;S) is not the finite marginal effect of making v a seed, which changes activation probabilities throughout the graph. The proposed hyperedge update is not derived from SICP, can treat a sum exceeding one as a probability, and is never checked against Monte Carlo activation probabilities or exact seed marginals. No guarantee applies to this method.","The empirical evidence is insufficient and partly circular. The supposedly real-world evaluations use real graph structures but simulated treatments/effects, and the paper does not clearly separate the estimator used for seed selection from the ITE values used for evaluation. There is no oracle policy regret, held-out outcome accuracy, uncertainty reporting, or statistical testing. Comparisons are limited mainly to unweighted greedy and random selection, omitting weighted-IM, causal-policy, nonmonotone optimization, and strong scalable IM baselines; A-CauIM is also worse than ordinary greedy on Contact.","Reproducibility and clarity are inadequate for the central claims: graph sizes, outcome-generation equations, estimator architecture, balancing loss, training protocol, constants C and Cd, convergence criteria, and complete hyperparameters are missing. Algorithm 1 contains undefined quantities and enforces only a one-sided ITE bound. strengths: The manuscript studies an important and potentially original problem: influence maximization when node utilities are heterogeneous, counterfactual, and sensitive to neighboring activation states, connecting network causal inference with hypergraph optimization. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/neurips2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-cglajmv5/call-07d129efae78459ca76c55863c9e3936/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
It presents both a simulation-based greedy method and a substantially faster vectorized heuristic, reflecting a useful accuracy-efficiency design goal.
The authors attempt to address difficult cases involving negative treatment effects and noisy effect estimates, rather than restricting attention to conventional fixed, nonnegative node weights.
The evaluation uses several graph structures and reports runtime, noise, and propagation-probability sensitivity; appendices and an anonymous code link also show some attention to reproducibility.
weaknesses: The causal objective is not correctly derived. Because tau_i depends on the realized neighboring treatment vector, the expected activated gain is E[1{T_i=1} tau_i(T_-i)], not ap(i;S)E[tau_i] without a conditional-independence argument. More generally, summing own-treatment contrasts does not equal the total policy effect under interference, which should compare aggregate potential outcomes under two treatment vectors. Thus the optimized quantity is not convincingly connected to the claimed profit or intervention benefit.

Identification is unsupported. Assumption 2.2 is written as independence between the two potential outcomes conditional on treatment and environment, rather than ignorability of treatment given pre-treatment covariates. Positivity, a valid exposure mapping, and support for environmental states induced by new seed policies are absent. A single factual outcome per node plus an HGCN does not by itself identify individual counterfactual effects, especially under network dependence and policy-induced distribution shift.

A central influence calculation is incorrect: ap(v;S) is defined as the sum of single-seed reachability probabilities, although reachability events from different seeds overlap and their probabilities cannot generally be added. Equation 7 repeats this additive decomposition and can double-count activated nodes. The subsequent approximation proof therefore does not apply to the stated diffusion model.

The theory analyzes fixed node weights, contradicting the paper's defining premise that treatment effects change with the environment and seed set. Even positive environment-dependent weights need not yield a submodular objective. The negative-weight bound relies on the erroneous fixed-weight decomposition, contains unjustified inequalities, can be vacuous through its unrestricted additive epsilon terms, and is inconsistent with the formulation allowing at most K seeds while the algorithm forces exactly K despite potentially negative marginal gains.

The robustness theorem uses multiplicative ratios involving sigma(S), which may be zero or negative in the setting explicitly emphasized by the paper; several inequality directions then cease to be valid. Its uniform relative-error premise is not linked to the pointwise ITE-error condition, and the Gaussian-noise experiment measures variance rather than regret against an oracle, so it does not validate the theorem.

A-CauIM is an unsupported heuristic rather than an accelerated implementation of greedy selection. The score (d sigma/d ap(v;S)) ap(v;S) is not the finite marginal effect of making v a seed, which changes activation probabilities throughout the graph. The proposed hyperedge update is not derived from SICP, can treat a sum exceeding one as a probability, and is never checked against Monte Carlo activation probabilities or exact seed marginals. No guarantee applies to this method.

The empirical evidence is insufficient and partly circular. The supposedly real-world evaluations use real graph structures but simulated treatments/effects, and the paper does not clearly separate the estimator used for seed selection from the ITE values used for evaluation. There is no oracle policy regret, held-out outcome accuracy, uncertainty reporting, or statistical testing. Comparisons are limited mainly to unweighted greedy and random selection, omitting weighted-IM, causal-policy, nonmonotone optimization, and strong scalable IM baselines; A-CauIM is also worse than ordinary greedy on Contact.

Reproducibility and clarity are inadequate for the central claims: graph sizes, outcome-generation equations, estimator architecture, balancing loss, training protocol, constants C and Cd, convergence criteria, and complete hyperparameters are missing. Algorithm 1 contains undefined quantities and enforces only a one-sided ITE bound. Runtime reporting excludes important costs and contains inconsistencies, including Torch 1.11 versus 2.1 and a caption claiming G-CauIM is faster when its table shows otherwise. Figure captions and dataset descriptions also conflict.

The practical health-outreach and marketing claims are not accompanied by analysis of fairness, consent, targeting harms, or sensitivity to biased causal estimates. No human intervention is performed here, so this is not an immediate ethical violation, but the omission weakens the claimed deployment relevance. Overall, the central formulation, guarantees, and empirical validation would all require substantial reconstruction rather than a rebuttal-scale clarification.
